title: A day built on prayer
hook: the five prayers as the frame of every day
tomorrow: one line in the dawn call isn't in any other. which one?

segments.voice: The commentators closed on one line: read with care, and with a teacher. Now a new block, Living It, and the part of Islam that happens five times a day.

Sunday night, a fresh planner, and every hour gets a color: class in blue, shifts in green, the gym in orange. By Wednesday the colors have bled into each other. Here's a much older schedule, and the story of how it was set. In a report kept in Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, on the night of his ascension, is given fifty prayers a day for his people. On the way down he meets Moses, who asks what he was given. Fifty, he says. And Moses answers: your people won't be able to bear it. Go back.
screen: `A PLANNER, BLEEDING COLORS.` → `FIFTY PRAYERS A DAY.` → `MOSES: GO BACK.`

segments.voice: So he goes back, and the number drops. Moses sends him back again, and again, until it reaches five. Even then Moses says ask once more, and the Prophet says he's too shy to ask again. Then the word comes: they are five, and they are fifty. Five to keep, with the reward of fifty. Those five are the frame Muslims build a day on: Fajr at dawn, Dhuhr at midday, 'Asr in the afternoon, Maghrib at sunset, 'Isha at night. The Qur'an puts it plainly, in Pickthall's words: "Lo! worship at fixed hours hath been enjoined on the believers." Fixed hours. Not whenever a minute opens up. Notice what that does to the planner. A lot of schedules start with the work and squeeze everything else into the gaps. This one starts with five posts driven into the ground, and the day gets built between them: class between Fajr and Dhuhr, a shift from Dhuhr to 'Asr. The posts move with the sun, a little earlier or later as the seasons turn, so the day keeps checking the sky and not only the clock. And the story leaves one detail worth telling a friend tonight: the five came out of a conversation, with Moses pushing for mercy. For the next two weeks, this block walks the day one post at a time.
screen: `FIFTY, THEN FIVE.` · `FAJR TO 'ISHA.` · `WORSHIP AT FIXED HOURS.` · `FIVE POSTS, THEN THE REST.` · then, large: `THE DAY HAS A FRAME.`

segments.voice: Take tomorrow, the real one, and find its five posts: about when dawn, midday, afternoon, sunset and night fall where you live. Put the five in first, then set your one biggest task between two of them, and notice what shifts. If you pray, those are your five; if not, they can be five short pauses.

segments.voice: A day built on prayer: five fixed posts from dawn to night, set in the story of fifty becoming five, and everything else fitted in between.

howItsDone: Muslims pray five daily prayers at times set by the sun: Fajr, Dhuhr, 'Asr, Maghrib and 'Isha. A mosque timetable or a prayer-time app gives each day's times, and people plan work, school and sleep around them.

trapdoor: what you thought: five prayers is five interruptions in a busy day.
what it means: the prayers are the frame; the day's work is built between five fixed posts.
what a scholar hears: Bukhari 349, fifty reduced to five ('they are five and they are fifty'), and Qur'an 4:103, kitaban mawqutan, prayer prescribed at set times.

chat.meaning: The Qur'an calls prayer worship at fixed hours. The five are the frame, so they go on the schedule first and everything else fits between.

Sahih al-Bukhari.meaning: a major collection of reports of the Prophet's words and deeds

Fajr.meaning: the dawn prayer, first of the five

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 349 (the ascension; fifty prayers reduced to five at Moses' urging; 'they are five and they are fifty')

notes: Confirm the exact Pickthall wording of 4:103's last clause.
Bukhari 349 (also Muslim 162/163) for the reduction from fifty to five; confirm the numbering and that 'too shy to ask again' fairly paraphrases the report.
'The posts move with the sun' is a general description of how prayer times are reckoned; no specific times given.
